audience.programmeDescription: Communication and Information Sciences at Tilburg studies how communication influences people, organisations and society. This Dutch-taught example follows Business Communication, selects Content Marketing and Analytics, Persuasive Design, Creativity and Cognition, and Misinformation and Polarization, and retains thirty credits for exchange study.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR can emphasise organisational and digital communication, communication for social impact, or human communication with cognitive and computational methods. Its courses offer substantial rhetorical, media and empirical inquiry. Tilburg has dedicated human-technology design, communication-research projects, generative-AI and strategic-communication courses, restricted electives and a required literature-review thesis. Relationships shown are partial.

componentNotes.y2-elective: Selected from the restricted second-year elective list. Content Marketing and Analytics is not repeated among the third-year choices.
componentNotes.y2-content: The research seminar collects and analyses language corpora, including manual and automated annotation, and reports a quantitative content analysis.
componentNotes.y3-minor: Thirty credits remain reserved for approved partner-university study. No destination or course package is imposed. The package must satisfy academic level, non-overlap and entry requirements.
componentNotes.y3-thesis: The twelve-credit thesis independently answers a communication-science question through a systematic literature review. Entry requires 120 programme credits including Academic Dutch, Academic English, Methodology, Statistics, Survey & Interview and Experiment. A proposal is assessed before the review and final report; an oral check follows.
componentNotes.y3-persuasive-design: Selected from the third-year restricted menu. It develops and evaluates a persuasive interaction design using psychological theory and user data.
componentNotes.y3-creativity: Selected as a second distinct third-year elective, studying cognitive processes and theories of creativity.
componentNotes.y3-misinformation: Selected as a third distinct third-year elective. Together these choices fill eighteen credits outside the completed Business Communication theme.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

BENENTR211.name: Marketing & Consumer Engagement
BENENTR211.text: Marketing & Consumer Engagement examines consumer psychology, marketing strategy, responsible brand development and customer engagement. Students analyse a company strategy, design a brand and investigate a consumer phenomenon using academic literature and primary and secondary evidence. Digital marketing and customer-journey mapping connect analysis with practical recommendations.

BENENTR212.text: The course explores how companies develop strategies and drive responsible digital transformation amid rapid technology change impacting the economy and society. Students develop a strategic plan, from vision to execution, and identify digital value opportunities. Using industry cases, they gain foresight into digital technologies and their impact on strategy, business models and social responsibilities.

HCBCOGN312.name: Psycholinguistics
HCBCOGN312.text: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.
